    NEEDS_HUMAN = "needs_human"    # low confidence, price, complaint
    QUOTED = "quoted"              # approved quote sent
    WON = "won"
    LOST = "lost"
    OPTED_OUT = "opted_out…

articles.author: Tech Geometry
articles.description:
AI is altering the way in which developers construct websites and web applications, and by 2026, AI coding assistants will be a common element of development workflows, aiding developers in writing code, correcting bugs, generating tests, and understanding complicated projects.
How AI Is Helping Web Developers
Faster Code Development
AI tools are able to suggest code, produce simple components, and assist developers in carrying out repetitive tasks. As a result, developers can devote more time to dealing with application logic and user experience.
Easier Debugging and Testing
Finding and fixing bugs gets simpler. You can test each part by itself. This helps you spot problems early. You save time and effort because you do not have to check the whole system at once.
AI can be used to spot possible errors, explain problems in the code, and propose test cases; yet developers must test the suggestions before using them in actual projects.
Better Website Experiences
Web applications can have AI-powered search, chatbots, recommendations, and content summaries provided by developers. Such features are useful to the extent that they address actual problems for users.
Why Human Skills Still Matter
AI-generated code isn't always correct, secure, or appropriate for a given project, and in order to evaluate the output properly, developers need to understand programming fundamentals, databases, APIs, performance, and security.
The 2026 Stack Overflow Developer Survey also points out the increasing role of AI coding tools and the need to verify their results.
Final Thoughts
AI is not merely taking the place of web developers; it is altering the way they work. Developers who use AI tools together with solid technical knowledge, thorough testing, and good problem-solving skills are able to create more reliable applications.
The aim must not be to write code as quickly as possible; it should be to produce websites and applications that are secure, useful, and easy to maintain.
articles.title: AI in Web Development in 2026: Faster Coding, Better Testing, and Human Review

The honesty problem in test-time compute


A lot of "reasoning engine" repos share two flaws: they never actually call a model, and they publish benchmark tables nobody can reproduce. HyperReason v1 was, by its own README's admission, exactly that.
v2.0.1 is a full honest rebuild: the engine genuinely drives real LLMs and publishes transparent evaluations — including runs where MCTS underperformed greedy decoding. No fake fallbacks; every number traces to code.
An adaptive-entropy Monte Carlo tree search engine for LLM test-time compute, on PyPI:

articles.author: Qingfeng
articles.description:
Normal debugging reads the log from the top: what did it try, what happened, where did it stop. That works when the failure is at the end, which is not where most of mine are.
Now I read the last line first, then the line that produced it, then walk backwards to the first decision that was wrong. The run usually failed at the top.
An agent that goes wrong at step two keeps going. It spends the rest of the run working on a false premise, and the last thing it does is the least informative thing in the file - an error on an already-wrong task.
Reading forwards, I walked through twenty correct-looking steps before reaching the failure. Reading backwards, I ask "what produced this state" at each step, and I arrive at the bad decision in three or four hops.
The first step whose input does not match what I expected. This is almost always the one, and it is usually a file read, a listing, or a state check.
The first step that silently changed something. Agents write files and start services; the log should say so. If a step has a side effect that is not in the log, that is a logging bug as well as a real one.
The last plausible command. Not the last command. The last one whose output would be different if the world were what I thought it was.
Once I was debugging this way, I stopped logging so much of the middle and started logging more at the boundaries: every read of external state, every side effect, the exact input that produced each decision. The middle steps are mostly derivable. The boundaries are not.
That is a small change with a large effect: my logs got shorter, and my time to find the wrong step went down, because the wrong step is almost always a boundary read that returned something I did not expect.
If you have done this long enough to have a rhythm, I am curious whether you walk forward or backwards. Mine was forwards for two months and it was costing me more than I noticed.
articles.title: I Read My Agent's Log Backwards, and the Bug Was in Line Two
